Northstar Dual-Fuel (LS-ND2)

The Northstar is our most repaired product by a wide margin, which is a function of how
many we sell and of how it is used, not of any weakness. Nearly every Northstar fault is one
of four things: a clogged generator, a dry pump cup, a torn mantle, or the wrong fuel. Ask
about the fuel first. The Northstar burns Clearburn white gas or unleaded gasoline. It does
not burn kerosene, and a tank that has had kerosene in it will have a varnished generator
and a sticky check valve. That is a paid repair even inside the warranty period.
Tools for the Northstar bench: 11 mm and 13 mm open-ended wrenches, the generator
wrench (part T-ND2, the thin 9 mm one with the bent handle), a small flat screwdriver, the
pump cup oil bottle, a nylon brush, and the torque driver set to 2.5 N·m for checking.
Generator tube replacement
The generator (part G-GEN2) is the tube that runs up through the burner and carries fuel
from the tank to the mantles. Signs of a bad generator are a weak yellow flame that will not
steady, pulsing light, and a tank that holds pressure but will not deliver it. The part is
$13.00, so a typical generator replacement on a yellow tag comes to $38.00 with the bench
fee.

1. Confirm the tank is drained and depressurised. Open the filler cap slowly over the tray.
2. Lift off the ventilator and the globe (part G-ND2). Set the globe on the padded shelf,
not on the bench.
3. Turn the control valve to the fully open position so the cleaning needle is clear of the
generator tip.
4. Loosen the generator nut at the base of the burner with the 11 mm wrench, then the
fitting at the valve body with the generator wrench. Draw the old generator straight up
and out.
5. Fit the new G-GEN2 with the tip toward the burner. Start both fittings by hand.
6. Tighten the valve body fitting hand-tight plus a quarter turn. Never more than 2.5
N·m. Check with the torque driver if you are new to this; the fitting is brass and strips
easily.
7. Tighten the generator nut the same way.
8. Pressurise with 20 strokes of the pump, no fuel in the tank, and soap-test both fittings.
Any bubbles, back off and reseat. Do not tighten further.
9. Fill with Clearburn white gas, fit the mantles, light under the hood and run the 30-
minute burn-in.

Pump cup service

The pump cup is the leather washer on the end of the plunger. When it is dry it will not seal
and the customer reports "the pump does nothing". Oil the pump cup with 3 drops of
Clearburn pump oil every 10 fills; tell the customer this on the return note, because it is the
one piece of maintenance that stops most Northstars coming back.
1. Unscrew the pump cap a quarter turn and withdraw the plunger.
2. Inspect the cup. A cup that is cracked or glazed hard is replaced (part P-CUP2); one
that is merely dry is oiled.
3. Put 3 drops of pump oil on the cup and work it in with your thumb until it is pliable.
4. Refit and pump 10 strokes. The resistance should build by the fourth stroke.

The Northstar is a pressurized dual-fuel lantern: you pump the tank, light the mantles, and get

## Fuel

### Can I burn kerosene in the Northstar?

No. The Northstar Dual-Fuel burns Clearburn white gas or unleaded gasoline only. Kerosene or
lamp oil will clog its generator in a single evening and the damage is not covered by warranty.

### What fuel goes in the Heritage No. 7?

Clearburn lamp oil only. Kerosene will burn but smokes, smells, and voids the 10-year warranty.

# Fuel Safety Guide

Last updated: June 2, 2026
Owner: Walt Brannigan, Head of Repairs

Lantern Supply Co. has sold fuel lanterns since 1987, and in that time the same handful of
mistakes have caused nearly every accident we have heard about: the wrong fuel, refuelling a hot
lantern, and fuel stored where it should not be. This guide covers what to burn in each product,
how to store and handle fuel, and what to do when something goes wrong. It applies to the
Northstar Dual-Fuel, the Hagerstown Kerosene Lantern and the Heritage No. 7 oil lamp. LED and
solar lanterns do not use fuel and are not covered here.

If you are ever unsure, do not light the lantern. Call us at (301) 555-0147 or email
help@lanternsupply.example and we will talk you through it.

## Approved fuels by product

Each fuel lantern is designed for a particular fuel, and the fuels are not interchangeable.
Using the wrong fuel is the most common cause of damage we see at the Repair Center, and
damage from an unapproved fuel is not covered by the warranty.

| Product | Approved fuel | Never use |
|---|---|---|
| Northstar Dual-Fuel (LS-ND2) | Clearburn white gas or unleaded gasoline | Kerosene, lamp oil |
| Hagerstown Kerosene Lantern (LS-HK12) | K-1 kerosene or Clearburn lamp oil | White gas, gasoline |
| Heritage No. 7 Brass Oil Lamp (LS-H7) | Clearburn lamp oil only | Kerosene, white gas |

The Northstar is called dual-fuel because it burns either Clearburn white gas or ordinary
unleaded gasoline from the pump. White gas burns cleaner and keeps the generator clear for
longer; unleaded is a fallback for when you cannot get white gas, not an everyday fuel. It must
never be fed kerosene. Kerosene will not vaporise in the Northstar's generator; it varnishes the
tube and sticks the check valve, and the lantern will need a paid repair.

The Hagerstown Kerosene Lantern is a wick lantern and burns K-1 kerosene, which is the clear,
low-sulphur grade sold for heaters, or Clearburn lamp oil. Lamp oil burns with less smell and
is the better choice indoors. Do not use white gas or gasoline in any wick lantern; both are
far too volatile for an open wick and the flame can run back into the tank.

The Heritage No. 7 burns Clearburn lamp oil only. Kerosene will work mechanically, but it
smokes, smells and stains the brass gallery, and scented or coloured decorative oils leave a
residue that clogs the wick. The 10-year Heritage Promise warranty does not cover damage from
any fuel other than lamp oil.
